chapters.title: The hero who built a wall of thorns

blocks.text: Alan Octavian Hume known in our history books as the man who gave Indians their political voice.  I grew up reading that too. It's only half the story. He engineered a living wall of thorns that cut entire subcontinent in two. A masterpiece of British engineering built not to stop an invading army but to tax salt. Behind it millions could not afford salt. Their bodies needed to survive. Today, nobody remembers the wall. Everybody remembers the hero.

This wall stretched 4,000 km across India. A British officer wrote that if you put it across Europe, it would reach all the way from London to Constantinople. 4,000 km of living thorns, cutting entire Indian subcontinent in two. Today, Indian history books remember Alan Hume as a hero who helped start Indian National Congress. And it was Hume who turned this giant wall into an impenetrable barrier. But Hume did not invent this wall. The British started it in 1840s by piling up thorny bushes along the

border. 20 years later, it still did not work. Just a broken line of dry twigs and  gaps anyone could step over. Then in 1867, Hume took charge. His job was to turn that broken hedge into a barrier no human could cross. And the British went to absurd lengths to build it. They wo together local babul thorns, plum shrubs, and jacked cactus into a wall up to 14 ft high, 12 ft thick. Along the patrol tracks, they planted towering tamarind trees to shade the

guards from the brutal sun. At places where geography is rocky, massive amount of soil was moved so the thorns could take root. Where rivers flooded the land, workers had to build high mud banks so plants would not drown. Where there was no water, laborers had to dug huge ponds to store monsoon rain. And where no plants could grow at all, they built stone walls. Every time nature gave a reason why a living wall could not work, the British engineered a way around it.

Between 1867 and 1870, Hume engineered over 1,600 kilometers of thick, impenetrable living thorns. 14,000 armed guards watched the line day and night. They stood in watchtowers every 2 km. They stopped every traveler. They tore open bags of food. They searched poor down to their clothes looking for a single grain of salt. Hume saw the human toll firsthand. In 1869, he filed an official report to the visory measuring salt consumption. Outside his wall, an

adult  ate 6 kg of salt a year. Inside the wall, less than four. Salt deprivation weakened people, made diseases harder to survive, and made effects of famine even worse. Which leaves one big question. Why was the exact same salt so cheap on one side of this barrier and an impossible luxury on the other? Because the British Raj was not one single country. People think British India had one law, one tax. It did not.

It was divided between British provinces and hundreds of independent princely kingdoms. In the kingdoms of Rajasthan, local rulers barely tax salt. A handful almost cost nothing. But just few steps across the British border, the colonial government placed a crushing tax on every  single grain. India never had a shortage of salt. In Rajasthan desert, lakes like sambar produced millions of tons of pure white salt every summer along thousands of kilometers of coastline. It dried under sun for free. Salt was everywhere. The

hedge existed to protect the price difference. A century earlier, Robert Clive took control of the salt trade for East India Company and made it a government monopoly. In Bengal, salt was taxed at 20 times it cost. A farm laborer earning two rupees a month buying salt took two full months of yearly wages. British policy made it impossible for poor people to effort. So traders went to work. They loaded  cheap salt from Rajasthan onto camels, bulockats and pack horses and

headed east towards British territory. The British called this traditional hereditary traders smugglers and criminals because cheap salt threatened colonial profits. The cost of this policy fell directly on ordinary people. First on the human body. See in India's brutal 45° heat, a laborer sweats out salt every hour. Without salt, human body cannot work and people quickly collapse from exhaustion. Second, on the animals, farm bulocks and cows grew weak

when farmers could not afford salt feed and cows produced less milk. And third, on daily life. The hedge sliced through villages, forcing farmers to walk miles to find armed gate.  Then in 1876, the monsoon failed. A catastrophic famine swept India. Widespread  salt starvation led to increased vulnerability to diseases like kolera. Millions perished. You would expect the British government to lower the salt tax to help dying people, right?

Instead, they increased it. Salt revenue climbed to 7 million pound sterling,  10 times what the wall cost to run. Yet inside the administration, officials grew uneasy. 14,000 guards and their English officers were expensive and they constantly took bribes and the smugglers, they always outsmarted the system. They climbed the hedge, launched bags of salt over it, floated salt past the checkpoints on unmanned rafts, and even disguised  it as dry fruits.

The hedge was becoming an expensive game of cat and mouse. And to be fair to the British, not all of them defended the hedge. Finance Minister Sir John Stratchy called it a monstrous system to which it would be almost impossible to find a parallel in any other country. The British wanted to get rid of embarrassing wall, but they refused to lose millions in revenue, which created a dilemma. How do you take down 4,000 km of wall without letting cheap salt flood

the country? Look at this map again. If British simply tore down the wall, cheap salt would immediately cross the border.  Smugglers would return and the British tax profits would crash. So the officials asked a simpler question. Instead of stopping the salt at the border, what if you control it before it ever leaves the ground? And in 1878, the British turned again to the man who had helped transform the hedge into an effective barrier. Alan Hume is now

a top official in British government. In 1878, the government sent Hume into Rajasthan on a highstakes mission. Hume met with local kings of seven different states. Under the threat of being deposed, Hume offered them a combined payout of nearly 23 lak rupees. In exchange for this money, the rulers signed treaties surrendering their independent salt manufacturing rights to British crown. In one stroke, Hume brought the biggest salt lakes and salt pans  in India under direct

British control. Under old system, salt was made by local workers, carried  by traders to the border, stopped by guards and taxed at the hedge. Under the new system, the British tax the salt directly at the source and this was made possible by new technology sweeping the subcontinent railways. The British laid train tracks straight onto salt beds of Sambar Lake. Workers shoveled salt into train wagons and the British collected the tax at source. The trains carried heavily taxed British salt into every town and villages,

wiping out local salt makers. The new system was cheaper, faster, and collected more money than a bushw wall ever could. So on the 1st of April 1879, the British government officially shut down the inland customs line. The hedge was gone, but the tax exploitation stayed. In fact, the British made salt taxes uniform across the country, causing the salt prices in southern and western India to double overnight. So where did 4,000 km of thorns go? Once the guards marched away, the local

villages came with access, clearing the dry bushes for firewood and dragging thorns to fence their fields. Farmers plowed the patrol paths into wheat fields. Within a generation, a 4,000 kilometers of living barrier vanished into the earth as if it never existed. In 1879, Hume lost his government post, retired to Shimla, and began organizing educated Indians. 6 years later 72 gathered in Bombay to launch Indian National Congress. Sitting in the front row is Alan Hume. History choose to
remember Alan Hume for the hall in Bombay. It completely forgot that for years he was the man who built, guarded and perfected the wall of thorns to exploit Indians.
